summary: Defines the first Management Information Base for TCP/IP network management, the list of things a device can report. It is a re-release of RFC 1066 with technical content unchanged. It is historic.

plainLanguage.summary: A checklist of facts a network device can tell you about itself, like how many messages it handled.

what is the original internet mib
subtitle: The first standard list of counters and settings that a TCP/IP device exposes to network management.

tldr.problem: Network operators needed a common set of variables to monitor and control hosts and gateways from different vendors, so that the same name means the same thing on every machine.
tldr.mechanism: The Internet MIB defines about a hundred essential objects in eight groups (System, Interfaces, Address Translation, IP, ICMP, TCP, UDP, EGP). Each object has a name, an ASN.1 syntax, an access mode and a status. If a group applies to a system, all of its objects must be implemented.
tldr.outcome: It is a re-release of RFC 1066 with unchanged technical content, and the unit metadata lists it as Historic.

sections.title: Where the MIB Fits
sections.content:
This memo is a re-release of RFC 1066 with a changed Status, IAB Policy Statement and Introduction, plus minor typographical corrections. The technical content is unchanged. It provides the initial Management Information Base (MIB) for network management of TCP/IP-based internets in the short term.

The management framework has three parts: RFC 1155 (how managed objects are defined, the Structure of Management Information), this memo (which objects exist), and RFC 1157 (the Simple Network Management Protocol, SNMP, which manages them). The IAB recommended that all IP and TCP implementations be network manageable, meaning they implement the MIB and at least one of SNMP or CMOT.

The introduction explains that the requirement for compatibility with both SNMP and the OSI management framework was suspended after RFC 1109 found the two frameworks more different than anticipated.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB is the list of questions you can ask a machine. A separate rulebook defines how to write questions, and another says how to ask them.

sections.title: Only the Essentials
sections.content:
The object list was derived by taking only elements considered essential, so no object is optional within a group it applies to. The primary criterion was being present in all of the earlier MIB definitions the group started from. The detailed criteria were:

  • Essential for fault or configuration management.
  • Only weak control objects, because current management protocols are not secure enough for powerful operations.
  • Evidence of current use and utility.
  • Limit the count to about 100 so vendors can fully instrument their software.
  • No object derivable from others.
  • No implementation-specific objects, such as for BSD UNIX.
  • Avoid heavily instrumenting critical code: about one counter per critical section per layer.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors packed a small bag with only what is truly needed, and nothing that could cause big trouble if someone fiddled with it.

sections.title: How Objects Are Described
sections.content:
Managed objects live in a virtual information store, the MIB, and are defined with ASN.1 (Abstract Syntax Notation One), restricted for simplicity. Each object type has a name (an object identifier, with a textual OBJECT DESCRIPTOR for convenience), a syntax and an encoding. The memo specifies the ASN.1 basic encoding rules.

Every definition has the same fields:

  • OBJECT: the descriptor and its identifier.
  • Syntax: the ASN.1 type, such as INTEGER, OCTET STRING, Counter, Gauge or TimeTicks.
  • Definition: the meaning, which must be consistent across machines in multi-vendor environments.
  • Access: read-only, read-write, write-only or not-accessible.
  • Status: mandatory, optional or obsolete.
sections.plainLanguage: Each question on the checklist has a name, a type of answer, a note on whether you may change it, and whether every device must answer it.

sections.title: The Eight Object Groups
sections.content:
Objects sit under mib, defined as { mgmt 1 }, in eight groups. Groups give a way to assign identifiers and tell an agent which objects it must implement: if a group applies, implement all of it. For example, the EGP group is needed if and only if EGP is implemented, and the TCP group applies to hosts running TCP.

  • System: sysDescr (printable ASCII description), sysObjectID (vendor identification under the enterprises subtree) and sysUpTime (hundredths of a second since the management portion was last re-initialized). Mandatory for all systems.
  • Interfaces: ifNumber and a table of interface entries with fields such as ifType, ifMtu, ifSpeed, ifAdminStatus and byte and packet counters.
  • Address Translation, IP (including ipForwarding, which says whether the entity acts as a gateway, the address table and the routing table), ICMP, TCP, UDP and EGP (with a neighbor table).

The TCP group includes tcpRtoAlgorithm, with values other, constant, rsre (MIL-STD-1778, Appendix B) and vanj (Van Jacobson's algorithm), and tcpConnState with the eleven connection states.
sections.plainLanguage: The checklist is split into chapters, one for each part of the machine, such as its network cards, its IP layer and its TCP layer. If you have the part, you answer the whole chapter.

sections.title: Growing the MIB
sections.content:
Keeping only essential objects is not restrictive, because the SMI offers three extension mechanisms. New standard objects can be added through new versions of the MIB. Widely available but non-standard objects can go in the multilateral subtree. Private objects go in the enterprises subtree. These can hold vendor-specific objects and also experiments to learn which other objects are essential.

The IAB policy statement adds that not every group is mandatory for every Internet component, and that more groups and variables are expected over time.
sections.plainLanguage: If you want more questions on your list, there are shelves for new official ones, shared extras, and your own private ones.

sections.title: Security
sections.content: The memo says only that security issues are not discussed in it. The one security-related design choice appears earlier: only weak control objects were allowed, because tampering with them can do only limited damage and the current management protocols are not sufficiently secure for more powerful control operations.
sections.plainLanguage: The authors did not add dangerous switches because the locks on the system were weak.
